{{Short description|Concepts in probability mathematics}}
{{Distinguish|Convergence of measures}}

'''Convergence in measure''' is either of two distinct mathematical concepts both of which generalize
the concept of [[convergence in probability]].

==Definitions==
Let <math>f, f_n\ (n \in \mathbb N): X \to \mathbb R</math> be [[measurable function]]s on a [[measure space]] <math>(X, \Sigma, \mu)</math>. The sequence <math>f_n</math> is said to '''{{visible anchor|converge globally in measure|Global convergence in measure}}''' to <math>f</math> if for every <math>\varepsilon > 0,</math>
<math display=block>\lim_{n\to\infty} \mu(\{x \in X: |f(x)-f_n(x)|\geq \varepsilon\}) = 0,</math>
and to '''{{visible anchor|converge locally in measure|Local convergence in measure}}''' to <math>f</math> if for every <math>\varepsilon>0</math> and every <math>F \in \Sigma</math> with
<math>\mu (F) < \infty,</math>
<math display=block>\lim_{n\to\infty} \mu(\{x \in F: |f(x)-f_n(x)|\geq \varepsilon\}) = 0.</math>

On a finite measure space, both notions are equivalent.  Otherwise, convergence in measure can refer to either global convergence in measure<ref name="Bogachev_2007">{{cite book |last1=Bogachev |first1=Vladimir Igorevich |title=Measure theory |date=2007 |publisher=Springer |location=Berlin New York |isbn=978-3-540-34514-5}}</ref>{{rp|2.2.3}} or local convergence in measure, depending on the author.

==Properties==
Throughout, <math>f</math> and <math>f_n</math> (<math>n\in\N</math>) are measurable functions <math>X\to\R</math>.

* Global convergence in measure implies local convergence in measure.  The converse, however, is false; ''i.e.'', local convergence in measure is strictly weaker than global convergence in measure, in general.
* If, however, <math>\mu (X)<\infty</math> or, more generally, if <math>f</math> and all the <math>f_n</math> vanish outside some set of finite measure, then the distinction between local and global convergence in measure disappears.
* If <math>\mu</math> is [[sigma-finite|''&sigma;''-finite]] and (''f''<sub>''n''</sub>) converges (locally or globally) to <math>f</math> in measure, there is a subsequence converging to <math>f</math> [[almost everywhere]].<ref name="Bogachev_2007" />{{rp|2.2.5}} The assumption of ''&sigma;''-finiteness is not necessary in the case of global convergence in measure.
* If <math>\mu</math> is <math>\sigma</math>-finite, <math>(f_n)</math> converges to <math>f</math> locally in measure [[if and only if]] every subsequence has in turn a subsequence that converges to <math>f</math> almost everywhere.
* In particular, if <math>(f_n)</math> converges to <math>f</math> almost everywhere, then <math>(f_n)</math> converges to <math>f</math> locally in measure.  The converse is false.
* [[Fatou's lemma]] and the [[monotone convergence theorem]] hold if almost everywhere convergence is replaced by (local or global) convergence in measure.
* If <math>\mu</math> is <math>\sigma</math>-finite, Lebesgue's [[dominated convergence theorem]] also holds if almost everywhere convergence is replaced by (local or global) convergence in measure.<ref name="Bogachev_2007" />{{rp|2.8.6}}
* If <math>X=[a,b]\subseteq\R</math> and ''&mu;'' is [[Lebesgue measure]], there are sequences <math>(g_n)</math> of step functions and <math>(h_n)</math> of continuous functions converging globally in measure to <math>f</math>. 
* If <math>f</math> and <math>f_n</math> are in [[Lp space|''L''<sup>''p''</sup>(''&mu;'')]] for some <math>p>0</math> and <math>(f_n)</math> converges to <math>f</math> in the <math>p</math>-norm, then <math>(f_n)</math> converges to <math>f</math> globally in measure. The converse is false.
* If <math>f_n</math> converges to <math>f</math> in measure and <math>g_n</math> converges to <math>g</math> in measure then <math>f_n+g_n</math> converges to <math>f+g</math> in measure. Additionally, if the measure space is finite, <math>f_n g_n</math> also converges to <math>fg</math>.

==Counterexamples==
Let <math>X = \Reals</math>, <math>\mu</math> be Lebesgue measure, and <math>f</math> the constant function with value zero.

* The sequence <math>f_n = \chi_{[n,\infty)}</math> converges to <math>f</math> locally in measure, but does not converge to <math>f</math> globally in measure.
* The sequence
::<math>f_n = \chi_{\left[\frac{j}{2^k},\frac{j+1}{2^k}\right]},</math> 
:where <math>k = \lfloor \log_2 n\rfloor</math> and <math>j=n-2^k</math>, the first five terms of which are 
::<math>\chi_{\left[0,1\right]}, \;\chi_{\left[0,\frac12\right]},\;\chi_{\left[\frac12,1\right]},\;\chi_{\left[0,\frac14\right]},\;\chi_{\left[\frac14,\frac12\right]},</math> 
:converges to <math>0</math> globally in measure; but for no <math>x</math> does <math>f_n(x)</math> converge to zero. Hence <math>(f_n)</math> fails to converge to <math>f</math> almost everywhere.<ref name="Bogachev_2007" />{{rp|2.2.4}}

* The sequence 
::<math>f_n = n\chi_{\left[0,\frac1n\right]}</math>
:converges to <math>f</math> almost everywhere and globally in measure, but not in the <math>p</math>-norm for any <math>p \geq 1</math>.

== Topology ==
There is a [[topological space|topology]], called the '''topology of (local) convergence in measure''', on the collection of measurable functions from ''X'' such that local convergence in measure corresponds to convergence on that topology.
This topology is defined by the family of [[pseudometric space|pseudometrics]]
<math display=block>\{\rho_F : F \in \Sigma,\ \mu (F) < \infty\},</math>
where
<math display=block>\rho_F(f,g) = \int_F \min\{|f-g|,1\}\, d\mu.</math>
In general, one may restrict oneself to some subfamily of sets ''F'' (instead of all possible subsets of finite measure). It suffices that for each <math>G\subset X</math> of finite measure and <math> \varepsilon > 0 </math> there exists ''F'' in the family such that <math>\mu(G\setminus F)<\varepsilon.</math> When <math> \mu(X) < \infty </math>, we may consider only one metric <math>\rho_X</math>, so the topology of convergence in finite measure is metrizable. If <math>\mu</math> is an arbitrary measure finite or not, then
<math display=block>d(f,g) := \inf\limits_{\delta>0} \mu(\{|f-g|\geq\delta\}) + \delta</math>
still defines a metric that generates the global convergence in measure.<ref>Vladimir I. Bogachev, Measure Theory Vol. I, Springer Science & Business Media, 2007</ref>

Because this topology is generated by a family of pseudometrics, it is [[uniform space|uniformizable]].
Working with uniform structures instead of topologies allows us to formulate [[uniform properties]] such as
[[Cauchy sequences|Cauchyness]].
